policy_title: Halt interest payments on QE reserves
stated: Reform UK will stop the Bank of England from paying interest to commercial banks on Quantitative Easing (QE) reserves, which they project would save around £35 billion per year.

source.quote: Bank of England Must Stop Paying Interest to Commercial Banks on QE Reserves This approach would save around £35 billion per year and has been endorsed by senior figures at the Financial Times, New Economics Foundation, and IFS, as well as two former Deputy Governors of the Bank of England.

bearing_set.reason: A projected £35bn annual saving/transfer creates very large fiscal space that could meaningfully raise household disposable income via tax cuts, while banks losing reserve income may compensate by widening lending/deposit spreads — both channels materially affect everyday household costs.

If commercial banks partially offset lost reserve income by raising mortgage lending rates, housing affordability (mortgage servicing costs) would be non-negligibly affected for existing and prospective homeowners.

Stopping ~£35bn/year interest payments on QE reserves would materially reduce the Treasury's fiscal drain (HM Treasury indemnifies BoE losses), directly affecting debt sustainability — a concrete, large-scale effect on public finances.

Interest on reserves is the Bank of England's primary monetary-policy floor instrument; removing it with ~£900bn+ of excess reserves outstanding risks disrupting credit conditions and monetary transmission, with plausible non-negligible effects on economic stability and real living standards.

membership_note: Two genuine bearings: a large direct fiscal effect (O12) and a plausible macroeconomic/monetary stability spillover (O13). Effects on individual household tax burden (O11) or cost of essentials (O2) are second-order and depend on contested bank pass-through assumptions that do not independently clear the non-negligible bar.
